summary:
The answer is what the Mortgage penalty calculator works out, and it gets there from the original mortgage principal, the outstanding mortgage balance and the annual prepayment privilege. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender.

Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Mortgage penalty calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mortgage penalty calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the mortgage type, the prepayment type and the payment frequency); then you give the mortgage maturity date; then you type in the original mortgage principal, the outstanding mortgage balance, the annual prepayment privilege and the current mortgage rate.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mortgage penalty calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Privilege amount=(original mortgage principal × annual prepayment privilege)
Total prepayment=(prepayment amount + how much have you prepaid since January 1st of this calendar year?)
Amount exceeding privilege=(-(original mortgage principal × annual prepayment privilege) + (prepayment amount + how much have you prepaid since January 1st of this calendar year?))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Mortgage type set to Fixed rate, Prepayment type set to Full, Original mortgage principal = 10 and Outstanding mortgage balance = 10. The calculator returns Privilege amount = 1, Total prepayment = 20 and Amount exceeding privilege = 19.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Privilege amount = 1, Total prepayment = 20 and Amount exceeding privilege = 19 should be roughly the size you expected from Mortgage type set to Fixed rate and Prepayment type set to Full.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mortgage penalty calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the original mortgage principal, the outstanding mortgage balance and the annual prepayment privilege — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Dates are compared date to date in your own time zone, so a daylight-saving change will not shift the count by a day.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mortgage penalty calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the original mortgage principal, the outstanding mortgage balance and the annual prepayment privilege, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter original mortgage principal in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Original mortgage principal opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Privilege amount = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Mortgage penalty calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
